bio.en: Matt MacInnis is the Chief Product Officer at Rippling, where he previously served as COO, and is known for his philosophy that extraordinary results require extraordinary effort.
bio.zh: 马特·麦金尼斯（Matt MacInnis）是 Rippling 的首席产品官，此前担任该公司 COO，以"非凡成果需要非凡投入"的理念而闻名。

summary.en: Matt argues you should deliberately understaff projects to avoid politics, cruft, and slowness that come with overstaffing. He insists the most selfish act is withholding feedback, because it optimizes for your own comfort at the team's expense. The episode is a demanding but energizing view of high-performance product culture.
summary.zh: 马特认为，应当刻意让项目"人手不足"，以避免过度配置带来的政治、冗余与迟缓。他坚持，最自私的行为就是隐瞒反馈，因为那是以团队为代价、优化自己的舒适。本期呈现了一种严苛却振奋人心的高绩效产品文化观。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: It is really important to me that we feel that we've deliberately understaffed every project at the company. If you overstaff, you get politics, you get people working on things that are further down the priority list than necessary. That is poison. It's wasteful. It slows you down. It creates cruft.
turns.zh: 对我来说，确保公司每个项目都合理配置人员至关重要。如果人员过剩，就会滋生办公室政治，让人们忙于处理那些优先级本应更低的工作。这种情况堪称毒瘤，既浪费资源又拖慢进度，还会滋生冗余。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been a long time COO at Rippling. Recently, you moved into CPO, Chief Product Officer at Rippling. Something you talk a lot about is that extraordinary results require extraordinary efforts.
turns.zh: 你担任Rippling的首席运营官已久，最近又晋升为首席产品官。其中一个你反复强调的观点是，非凡的成果需要付出非凡的努力。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: If you want to be in the 99th percentile in terms of outcomes, it's going to be really difficult. You got to sort of remind people that if they ever find themselves in the comfort zone at work, they are definitely making a mistake. It's supposed to be really fricking exhausting.
turns.zh: 若想在成果上达到99%的水准，难度极大。你得不断提醒人们，若在工作中陷入舒适区，那就是在犯错。工作本该令人精疲力竭。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're a big fan of escalating issues.
turns.zh: 你很推崇将问题上报的做法。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Fundamentally, the most selfish thing you can do is withhold feedback from someone. When you think a thought that would help someone improve and you avoid giving it to them because it would make you uncomfortable. Well, you're optimizing for your own comfort, and it's fundamentally selfish. So many people have teams that are not functioning incredibly well. Teams will always optimize for local comfort over company outcomes. The purest form of ambition and most intense source of energy in the business is the founder CEO. Every next concentric circle of management beyond the founder CEO has the potential to be an order of magnitude drop off in intensity. That is fucking dangerous. (00:01:17): As an executive, as a leader, your job is to preserve that intensity at its highest possible level. You've had a couple really interesting experiences with your own startup. We talk in Silicon Valley about never quit, but that is complete absolute venture capital.
turns.zh: 从根本上讲，隐瞒反馈是最自私的行为。当你有能帮助他人进步的想法，却因顾虑面子而选择沉默时，这就是在为自己的舒适而优化，实质上是自私的。许多团队运作不畅，因为他们总是优先考虑本地舒适感而非公司利益。创始人CEO是商业中最纯粹的雄心和最强劲的能量源泉。除创始人CEO之外的每一层管理层，其激情都可能呈指数级衰减。这太他妈危险了。（00:01:17）作为高管和领导者，你的职责是将这种激情维持在最高水平。你在自己的创业公司有过一些非常有趣的经历。我们在硅谷常说永不放弃，但那完全是风险投资的套路。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: This is a term, that phrasing I actually attribute to a friend of mine, Dan Gill, who's the chief product officer at Carvana, which as a company also doesn't get enough credit for how much of a tech company it actually is. Super interesting. And I think as a general framework for me, and a lot of what I say with you today is not really specific to product in any way. We should actually talk about that. It's like the product function is an instantiation of the general concept of management. Being a chief product officer is not that different from being a chief whatever officer. You have to apply the same frameworks and concepts to get people to achieve goals together. But one thing that is absolutely universal that I think we, honestly, I think we forget it in Silicon Valley or a lot of people don't sort of internalize it, is that if you want to accomplish something truly extraordinary, if you want to be in the 99th percentile in terms of outcomes, it's going to be really difficult. (00:05:56): It's going to be really uncomfortable. And you got to sort of remind people of that, that if they ever find themselves in the comfort zone at work, they are definitely making a mistake. They have definitely screwed up somehow. It's not that an extraordinary effort is sufficient to an extraordinary outcome, but it is 100% true that it is necessary. And so I do use that framework as a sort of guiding principle in my own leadership.
turns.zh: 这是一个术语，这个说法实际上来自我的朋友丹·吉尔（Dan Gill），他是Carvana公司的首席产品官。这家公司作为科技公司，其成就并未得到充分认可，这真的很有意思。对我而言，这是一个通用的框架，我今天与大家分享的很多观点都并非专属于产品领域。我们应该深入探讨这一点——产品职能本质上是管理这一普遍概念的具体化。首席产品官与其他任何职位头衔的本质并无太大差异。无论担任何种职位，都需要运用相同的框架和理念，推动团队共同达成目标。但有一条绝对普适的真理，我认为我们在硅谷或其他地方往往忽视了它：若想取得非凡成就，若想在成果层面跻身前1%行列，必定会面临巨大的挑战，过程注定充满不适。我们必须时刻提醒人们：当他们在工作中陷入舒适区时，就肯定犯了错。仅付出平庸努力绝非能收获非凡成果，但可以百分之百确定的是，付出非凡努力是实现非凡成果的必要条件。因此，我将这套思维框架视为自己领导力的核心准则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make this even more real for people, what are examples of moments that were extraordinarily hard?
turns.zh: 为了让大家更真切理解这一点，你能举些极其艰难的时刻案例吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: It is not about any sort of grand single story. I think the story is actually told through a thousand little things. And so for me, the story is told through a thousand Jira tickets, not through a thousand grand events. The extraordinary effort thing is a reminder that it's supposed to be really fricking exhausting. It's supposed to be. So on Friday night, when you get hit with an escalation on Friday night, when you get sort of hit with a bunch of new bugs from someone in the engineering team that you've got a triage, those are the moments where great players and great teams are separated from good players and good teams. And it's so easy to say this at a company like Rippling because we're winning. As a company, for all of our foibles, and we should spend time today talking about where things are not perfect and not great, but the growth rate of the company on the revenue foundation that we have is extraordinary, really, really compelling. (00:07:33): And it gives you, as a leader, the air cover to get up in front of your team and say, "Hey guys, I need the last ounce of oil that you've got left." And if your company's not growing very quickly, if things aren't that great, if your growth rate is 30% or 40%, it doesn't feel as good as a contributor in that business to lean in and give everything you've got on Friday or Saturday or Sunday because you don't know that it's going to yield much. And so extraordinary results, outcomes demand extraordinary efforts, but if there's no chance at an extraordinary outcome, it's very hard to get the extraordinary effort. And so I like to remind people at Rippling at least that it's so rare to have the opportunity to be able to be a part of a team where the extraordinary effort that you do put in on Friday or whatever, whenever it is actually contributing to an extraordinary result. (00:08:27): It's a very special and rare thing, and it gives me a superpower as a leader because I can lean on that when I'm ringing the oil out of somebody who's in the bored and tired zone.
turns.zh: 这无关乎任何宏大的单一叙事。我认为故事实际上是通过千千万万个微小细节来呈现的。于我而言，这个故事是通过数千张Jira工单来讲述的，而非通过千百场盛大事件。这种非凡的努力时刻提醒着我们，成功注定是异常艰辛的。周五晚上，当你接到升级请求，当你被工程团队成员抛来一堆新漏洞需要紧急处理时——这些正是区分优秀玩家与普通玩家的关键时刻。在Rippling这样的公司说这番话很容易，因为我们正在赢得胜利。尽管我们存在种种不足，今天我们也应该花时间讨论哪些方面尚未尽善尽美，但基于现有营收基础的公司增长速度堪称非凡，着实令人振奋。（00:07:33）作为领导者，这赋予了你足够的底气站在团队面前说：“嘿，伙计们，我需要你们最后一滴油。”但如果公司增长速度不够快，如果情况不尽如人意，如果增长率仅为30%或40%，那么在周五、周六或周日全力以赴的贡献者们就很难感受到那种成就感，因为他们不确定自己的付出能换来多大回报。因此，非凡的成果需要非凡的努力，但如果没有非凡的结果可期，要获得这种非凡的努力就极为困难。所以我在Rippling至少会提醒大家，能成为一个团队中的一员的机会实属难得——当你在周五或其他任何时候付出非凡努力时，若能为非凡的成果添砖加瓦，那真是件特别而难得的事。（00:08:27）这是一件非常特别且难得的事，作为领导者，这赋予了我一种超能力——当我要从那些身处倦怠疲惫区的成员身上榨出最后一滴油时，我能依赖这种力量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw the same thing actually at Airbnb with Brian Chesky. It always felt like things were going great and maybe we could take a break after something we shipped was killing it. And it always felt like the opposite. It always felt like, how do we press the gas pedal further? How do we go faster? How do we go bigger? There's never a moment to take a break.
turns.zh: 实际上，我在Airbnb与布莱恩·切斯基共事时也见证过类似的情况。事情总是一帆风顺，似乎我们在某个产品上线大获成功后就能松口气。但事实恰恰相反。问题总是在于：我们如何能再踩大油门？如何能更快前进？如何能做得更大？从没有片刻可以松懈。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I spent seven years at Apple and learned under Steve Jobs when he was the CEO, learned what we called the death march, which is what we did to the engineers. It was like as soon as you shipped one version of the iPhone, you were just immediately thrown into the pit of building the next one and there was no break. It was just relentless and talk about an extraordinary outcome at the end of the day. There is no relief. In a competitive market, and if the market is valuable, it's competitive, no question. If you leave anything on the field, if you sort of leave a crack for your competitor, 100% chance they're going to go fill that crack. And so you have to be relentless. There can be no relaxation of the organization. It doesn't mean people can't come and go or people can't take vacations or live their lives, of course. (00:09:48): And it's not like people are human beings. You can't grind the individuals down, but the team as a collective group of people has to be sort of on the ball all the time. There can't be a break. And if you leave one, you're just begging for the slightly more hungry competitor to come in and eat your lunch. And that's the beauty of capitalism.
turns.zh:
我在苹果公司工作了七年，师从乔布斯担任CEO时期，深刻领悟了我们所说的"死亡行军"——即对工程师们近乎无情的压榨。只要你交付了一个iPhone版本，紧接着就被投入到下一个版本的开发中，中间没有任何喘息的机会。这是一种永无止境的循环，最终却能造就非凡的成果。没有任何缓冲空间。在竞争激烈的市场中，只要市场有价值，竞争就必不可少。若你留有任何漏洞，竞争对手必将无缝填补。因此，组织必须保持持续高压。当然，这并不意味着员工不能离职、休假或享受生活。

（00:09:48）人毕竟是人。你不能把个人压榨至极限，但整个团队必须时刻保持警觉，容不得半点懈怠。一旦出现松懈，稍微更具野心的竞争对手就会趁虚而入。这正是资本主义的魅力所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, very counterintuitively, and maybe the more optimistic perspective here is when you do give your team space to just twiddle their thumbs, bad things start to happen. Morale actually dips in my experience. People get distracted. They're like, "Oh, what are we even doing? It's not interesting." I find that keeping people busy and motivated and fired up, even though you may think they'll be happier taking a many week break and slowing things down, I find they get more, the more I actually goes down in those moments.
turns.zh: 相反，一个看似矛盾却更乐观的观点是，当你给团队留出空闲时间时，反而会引发问题。以我的经验来看，士气会直线下降。员工容易分心，会质疑："我们到底在做什么？这根本没意思。" 我发现，即便员工认为休假数周放慢节奏更幸福，但在高强度工作中激发他们的斗志，反而能让他们收获更多。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: So here's a management framework that I use fairly often. As an executive, you don't know how to get any decision exactly right. It's not knowable. You don't know how much budget to allocate. You don't know how many people to put on a project. You don't know how to set a deadline for when you're going to ship something. But of course, you have to set some default so you make your best guess and then you manage to that best guess and you learn as you go because in software development and in business in general, everything's emergent. These are not things that are knowable top down or a priority. And so you take a best guess and knowing that you're not going to get the right answer, you need to decide whether over-steering or under-steering relative to your perceived midpoint is better. And so let's talk about staffing. When you staff a project, is it better to overstaff or is it better to under-staff knowing that you can't get it right? Well, it's better to under-staff. If you overstaff, you get everything that you just said. You get politics, you get people working, I think most importantly on things that are further down the priority list than necessary. You have like 20 things on a stack rank list and you know that you got to do the top five, but the next 15 data's kind of ambiguous, but you've overstaffed the project. So the next 10 things down are getting worked on. Before you even know if they're necessary, that is poison. It's wasteful, it slows you down, it creates crust. And so it's very clear that under-staffing is less evil than over-staffing. In this particular framework, the advice is under-staff deliberately, always. And then the wisdom, the wisdom element is to know not to under-under-staff and sort of knowing the difference between those two things. (00:12:22): And so that's the way we work at Rippling. Everyone is constantly asking for more resources and of course where we can afford to and where it's appropriate new resources arrive, but it is really important to me that we feel that we've deliberately understaffed every project at the company.
turns.zh: 以下是我经常使用的一个管理框架。作为高管，你无法做到每个决策都尽善尽美。这是不可知的。你不知道该分配多少预算，不知道一个项目需要多少人手，也不知道什么时候设定交付期限。但当然，你必须设定一个默认值——尽可能做出最佳猜测，然后围绕这个猜测进行管理。在学习过程中不断调整，因为在软件开发和商业领域，一切都是不断涌现的。这些事情不是自上而下就能预测的，也不是优先级最高的任务。所以你做出最佳猜测，知道自己不可能得到正确答案后，就需要判断相对于感知的中点，是过度管控还是不足管控更好。接下来谈谈人员配置问题。当为一个项目配置人员时，过度配置还是不足配置更好？显然不足配置更优。如果过度配置，你会遇到上述种种问题：政治斗争、人们忙于处理优先级较低的任务等。比如优先级排序列表上有20项任务，你知道必须完成前五项，但后15项数据模糊不清，却为项目过度配置了人力。这样一来，后10项任务就被提上日程，而你甚至还不知道它们是否有必要。这简直是毒药。既浪费资源，又拖慢进度，形成恶性循环。因此，显然不足配置比过度配置危害更小。在这个框架中，建议是故意不足配置人员，始终如此。关键在于要知道何时不应不足配置，并能区分这两者的区别。（00:12:22）这就是我们在Rippling的工作方式。每个人都在不断要求更多资源，当然在我们负担得起且合适的情况下，新资源也会加入，但对我来说，重要的是要确保公司里的每个项目都经过了刻意的人员不足配置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a previous guest, I forget who this was. They used this metaphor if they want their team to be dehydrated to always be wanting more water. And then eventually they're too dehydrated and okay, we needed someone to help. Interesting. Yeah. There's a line along the lines of extraordinary efforts I want to make sure I read because I think this is really good. This may be a way to summarize what you're saying, that good teams get tired and that's when great teams kick the good team's asses.
turns.zh: 之前有位嘉宾，我忘了是谁。他们用了一个比喻，如果想让团队像脱水的人一样不断渴望更多水源。结果最终他们脱水过度，无奈之下才引入外援。挺有意思的。是的。有句话大意是，想要做出非凡努力，我一定要记住，因为我觉得这很棒。这或许能总结你的观点，即优秀团队会疲惫不堪，而卓越团队则会超越他们。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yes. This was a quote actually from Sunil, and he found it from a women's basketball team coach. And it is, to my point earlier about you got to run the engine at the red line at all times because the minute you let your guard down, the minute you slow down, the minute you relax, the minute you leave a crack for your competition, the great teams are going to come in and kick the good team's. And it's like sports, I'm not a very sporty guy, but sports analogies are sort of irresistible because at the end of the day, business is a game and none of this matters. We're not going to carry it to the grave. It's like you're here to do this stuff because it somehow fulfills you while you're on the planet. And I love the sport of business and I find that sports, notwithstanding the fact that I watched very little of it, that military, those are very ripe sources of parallel concepts to apply in leadership.
turns.zh: 是的。这句话实际上是苏尼尔引用的一位女子篮球队教练的话。正如我之前所说，企业必须时刻保持全速前进，因为一旦你放松警惕、放慢脚步、松懈懈怠，一旦给竞争对手留下一丝可乘之机，那些优秀的团队就会乘虚而入，击败你。虽然我不太热衷体育，但体育类比确实很有感染力——毕竟商业本质上也是一场竞赛，这些道理终究会随风而逝。正如你所说，我们做这一切的初衷，是为了在世间留下自己的价值。我热爱商业这项运动，即便我看体育赛事的机会不多，但军事领域同样能为领导力提供诸多启示。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I find also those most intense, stressful, long nights are the moments you remember most and remember most fondly back to when you're building something. The key though is that it has to go well. As you said, if you are succeeding and winning, all of this is romantic in the end and nostalgic. Remember that time we built this thing and worked late nights and shipped this thing? If it doesn't go anywhere, you don't feel that. So I think that's a really important component of this is you need to be winning and succeeding.
turns.zh: 我发现，那些最紧张、最充满压力、最漫长的夜晚，往往是创业者最难忘、最怀念的时刻。关键在于事情必须进展顺利。正如你所说，如果成功了，一切都变得美好而令人回味。比如我们曾通宵达旦打造出这款产品，那段时光多么难忘。但如果项目最终胎死腹中，就感受不到那种激情。所以，成功与胜利才是这一切的核心要素。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: One thing that I've learned from Parker, Parker's our CEO at Rippling, he said, "You don't really learn from your mistakes, you learn from your successes." And it's like you do, of course, and he would admit you learn a bit from mistakes, but I do think that this is sort of feel good that it's like, "Well, you didn't succeed, but at least you learned something." I've had failures. When I look back at the nine years I spent working on inkling from day one in 2009 until we sold that business to a private equity firm in 2018, up the curve of Silicon Valley coolness, back down the other side into obscurity. Of course, I learned and grew a ton during that time, but in now what I think is six or seven years, I'm trying to do the math, seven years coming up on at Rippling, I've learned so much more because I've seen success. (00:15:13): I've seen rapid, wild, crazy off the charts success of the business and it's more informative. There's more to glean from seeing how it's done right than there is to glean from seeing how it's done wrong. If I tell you you're going to get on an airplane and one maintenance technician has seen it done right a hundred times and the other maintenance technician has seen it done wrong a hundred times, but he learned from his mistakes, but still hasn't had any success himself. I mean, give me a break. There's not even a comparison which plane you're going to feel more comfortable on. And so I do think that learning from your mistakes thing is a bit of a feel good trope that actually has very little substance in reality. And it's why as an early career product manager, or it's why frankly at any stage of your career when you want to learn, you should join a winning team. (00:15:57): It's cool to go and start a company at 22. Good luck to you. The odds are not in your favor, but the folks who, when I look at a resume and I see that someone's joined, they were at really good companies when those companies were super exciting and in crazy growth mode. I'm like, "I instantly want to interview that candidate because I want to hear what they learned from being part of a winning team." And that's sort of one of my go to heuristics when I'm looking at candidate profiles and I think it's an under-told trope. Sorry, not an under-told trope. It's a piece of advice that I don't think people embrace enough in the valley that success begets success and you should chase success.
turns.zh: 关于成功和学习，我从帕克那里学到的一点是——帕克是Rippling的首席执行官。他说：“你其实不是从错误中学习，而是从成功中学习。” 当然，你确实能从错误中吸取教训，但我认为这更多是一种自我安慰的心态，类似于“虽然你没有成功，但至少学到了些东西”。我也经历过失败。回顾2009年从inkling项目第一天到2018年将业务出售给私募股权公司的这九年历程，我们见证了硅谷科技公司的兴衰起落。当然，这期间我也成长了许多，但在过去的六七年里——我算算，加入Rippling快七年了——我学到的东西更多，因为我亲眼见证了成功。（00:15:13）我见证了业务飞速发展、势如破竹般的成功，这比从失败中吸取教训更有启发。想象一下：如果你要坐飞机，一个维修技术人员已经成功操作过一百次，而另一个技术人员却犯过一百次错误，但他只从错误中吸取了教训，却从未真正成功过——拜托，这根本没法比。很显然，你会更愿意乘坐前者的飞机。正因如此，我认为从错误中学习这种说法更多是自我安慰，现实中其实意义不大。这就是为什么作为初级产品经理，或者说在任何职业阶段，如果你想学习成长，都应该加入一个成功的团队。（00:15:57）22岁就创办公司很酷，祝你好运。但成功率确实不高。但那些简历上写着曾在非常热门、处于疯狂增长阶段的优秀公司工作过的人，我会立刻想约他们面试，因为我想听听他们在成功团队中学到了什么。这是我看候选人简介时常用的判断标准，我觉得这是一个被忽视的真理。抱歉，不是被忽视的真理。而是硅谷里人们没有充分重视的一个道理：成功会孕育成功，你应该追逐成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of success and learning, you've been a long time COO at Rippling and the reason you're here recently you moved into CPO, chief product officer at Rippling, which is very exciting and very rare. I don't see a lot of COOs moving into product. Let me ask you why did you move into that role? I feel like you've been killing it at COO. Maybe that's the reason. Be careful what you're good at. And also just what are some surprises about this, about moving into product? Because a lot of people imagine what it's like and then you're actually doing it.
turns.zh: 说到成功和学习，你在Rippling担任了很久的COO，最近又晋升为CPO，首席产品官，这非常令人兴奋，也很罕见。我没见过很多COO转到产品岗位的。我想问问你为什么会转到这个角色？我觉得你之前做COO已经做得很出色了。也许这就是原因吧。要小心你擅长的东西。还有，转到产品岗位有什么惊喜吗？因为很多人对此有想象，但实际做起来才发现不同。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: The story at Rippling is pretty interesting and I'll tell it because I think it explains why I'm making this transition, but this isn't really about me. I think it's sort of a pattern that your listeners would find useful. In general, your best executives are the ones that you can mostly toss into any challenge and they will bring order to chaos. They will fix the thing. And I do appreciate the terms that people have used at Rippling for me, talking about MacInnis's injured birds, where at any given moment some function is in disarray or in jeopardy and I go and focus very carefully on that function to get it back in order batting 800 maybe, like not always wild success, but I did that everywhere except R&D. I would think about helping out with components of the sales organization like our channel team, or I spent time building out the recruiting function a few times when it needed to be sort of rethought in response to our growth, but it never R&D. (00:18:23): And so I would have my feet up on the table looking out across the floor at this dumpster fire off in the distance, just sort of emitting smoke and wondering if someone was going to go in and deal with that. And the smoke takes various forms and when you're growing as quickly as rippling is growing, it's not always something that necessarily even impacts customers, but it's the sort of thing where you're like, that architecture's not right or they're not measuring adoption correctly." From the outside, I actually had quite a few criticisms that I could lob in. And what happened at Rippling was we made some hiring mistakes. I think the folks that we had in those roles would agree that they weren't the right people. We had a hiring mistake in engineering leadership where the product leader at the time had to sort of run engineering. (00:19:07): We subsequently had a mistake in product hiring and a lot of us had to sort of pitch in. And Parker and I sort of stared at each other through two years of this kind of disarray or this chaos or this agony of things and just never really having good executive leadership over both engineering and product at the same time. And I remember Parker sort of slumped down in his seat and said, "Oh, I have to run another search." And I said, "No, the gig's up. I'm going to go do it." And he really sprung up in his seat. He's like, "Really? You'll go do that?" I'm like, "Dude, this is what the business needs." And so that's what I did. And that really started about a year ago in sort of, I realized I was going to do it and expressed that to Parker in December. I really took it on in January of '25. (00:19:51): And so it's been 11 months of learning. Jumping into the product role when the product function itself, although staffed with really talented people, wildly under understaffed, and without a single spiritual leader on top of it to drive consistency and process excellence had become locally optimized but globally incoherent. And if you know Conway's law, you are destined to ship your org chart. And so with a locally optimized, globally incoherent team, you had a locally optimized, globally incoherent product experience that needed to be resolved. And so my efforts over the last 11 months have been to establish greater clarity in terms of how we do things around here, better process, better general leadership, hiring and firing. I mean, just doing the sort of cleanup on aisle three that needed to be done, even though, again, a lot of the people in the team were quite talented and doing an excellent job of managing their specific domains. (00:20:52): Jumping into the product role has been quite eye-opening. I feel a little bashful about the naivety of my view from the outside a year ago. Product teams have a hierarchy of needs, and we like to point at the failures to meet elements of that hierarchy higher up the triangle and sort of impugn the failure of that organization for not, as an example, measuring adoption metrics very carefully and not closely tracking those metrics as a means by which to drive execution. When I jumped in, I was like, "Man, we need to establish some basic standards for test coverage. We need to establish some basic standards for how we do what I call a factory inspection on a product once it's ready to roll off the assembly line." Do we have a checklist for what we call product quality and what does product quality mean? Those basic things weren't there. And so the idea that we should be spending time measuring adoption metrics is absolute insanity. (00:22:08): You're skipping a lot of steps between here and there. And so we have made great strides and I think it's translating to product quality improvements for our customers, but I feel, as I said, a little dumb for the way I was thinking about it before I jumped into the deep end. There is just no excuse as an executive for sitting outside of the mess and thinking you know the answers. It's a cardinal sin as an executive to do that. You need to go and see. You'd be in the boiler room, you need to study the system, bottom up and develop hypotheses for how to amend the system. And that's what I've been doing.
turns.zh:
瑞普林（Rippling）的故事相当有趣，我之所以要讲述它，是因为我觉得这能解释我为何会做出如今的转变，但重点其实不在我个人。我认为听众会发现其中蕴含一种模式——最优秀的高管往往能在任何挑战面前从容应对，他们总能化解混乱，扭转局面。我很感激瑞普林团队用"麦金尼斯受伤的鸟儿"来形容我，意思是某个职能部门陷入混乱或面临危机时，我会全力以赴重整旗鼓。除了研发部门，我在其他所有领域都能做到这一点——比如帮助渠道团队重建销售组织，应对增长挑战时重新设计招聘流程等。但唯独研发部门始终未能达成目标。

（00:18:23）有时我会坐在桌前，看着远处如火如荼的混乱局面，烟雾缭绕却不见人去灭火。这些问题形态各异，但随着瑞普林发展迅速，许多问题并未直接影响客户——比如架构不合理、数据采集不准确等。而外界对我们的批评也接踵而至。核心问题在于招聘失误：工程团队领导接手产品线时，工程部门已然陷入瘫痪；产品团队招聘失误后，我们不得不全员参与救火。帕克和我在两年混乱中相互注视，却始终缺少同时掌控工程与产品的高管人才。记得帕克曾瘫倒在椅子上说："又要重新招人了。"我说："不行，时候到了。"他猛地坐直："真的吗？你要亲自上阵？"我说："兄弟，公司需要你这样做。"

于是过去一年间，我全力投入。去年12月向帕克表态，今年1月正式接管。11个月的学习之旅中，产品团队虽人才济济，却严重人手不足，缺乏统一的流程指导。按照康威定律，组织架构注定会杂乱无章。面对本地优化却全球割裂的局面，我必须重构产品体验。过去一年，我致力于建立清晰的管理规范、优化流程、强化领导力体系，进行人员优胜劣汰。就像清理三号过道的积灰，虽然团队成员大多才华横溢，但他们在各自领域的卓越表现掩盖了整体架构的混乱。
（00:20:52）：转入产品角色后，我深有感触。回想一年前作为局外人时的天真想法，现在觉得有点难为情。产品团队有需求层级，我们总爱把未能满足高层需求归咎于组织失败。比如，某个组织未能精确衡量产品采用率指标，也未能密切追踪这些数据以推动执行——这简直太离谱了。刚入行时，我曾想：“天哪，我们得制定测试覆盖率的基本标准。产品下线前，我们得进行‘出厂检查’般的质量把关。”但根本没有产品质量的标准清单，更遑谈衡量采用率指标。当时我觉得这简直是疯了。  
（00:22:08）：从那到现在，我们跨越了许多阶段。如今我们在产品质量提升方面取得了显著成效，这对客户来说意义非凡。但正如我所说，我之前的思维方式实在太幼稚了。作为高管，绝不能隔岸观火，自以为无所不知。这是高管的致命错误。你必须深入实地，亲自研究。就像在锅炉房里操作一样，得从底层开始，逐步分析系统，形成改进假设。这正是我一直在做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love hearing this because so many people have teams that are not functioning incredibly well and hearing from someone that is not a longtime product person come in and try to fix these problems, I think is really useful and interesting for people to hear. To dig into this a little bit more, was the big lesson and kind of eye-opening moment that there's a lot of foundational work that needs to happen to achieve this outcome that you're trying to achieve, which is measure engagement and adoption well? Is it like tracking and metrics and data science? Is that kind of the lesson there?
turns.zh: 我很乐意听别人分享这些见解，因为很多团队的运作效率并不理想。听一位非产品出身的人尝试解决这些问题，我觉得这对大家来说既有启发又很有价值。具体来说，最大的收获在于：要实现衡量用户参与度和产品采用率这样的目标，需要先做好基础工作。比如追踪数据、分析指标、应用数据科学等，这些都是关键的策略。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: The lesson is that everything must be done in its time and order, and you can move really, really quickly. There's no sort of excuse not to move with urgency on all of these things, but you got to do them in order and you have to lead bottom up. You got to lead from the specific circumstances you observe. And I think for me, one of the best things that's happened over the last 11 months is that I've gained a greater trust in my own instincts, that sort of patterns I've matched across other functions do indeed apply in product, but I have both the advantage and disadvantage of not having led a product function before and therefore must think about every problem from first principles. I have no choice. I can read shit on the internet. I can listen to clear thinkers on topics and import their ideas, but I'm very reluctant to import an idea without breaking it down into its constituent parts and figuring out how it applies at Rippling. (00:24:29): And so I don't actually give a shit about adoption metrics as a matter of principle. I care about adoption metrics when I care about adoption metrics. I realize that that's a total logical statement, but it's like I'll get there. And so in certain parts of our product, I really do care about adoption metrics. I care a lot about adoption metrics in our applicant tracking system, our recruiting product, because it's in a really good place from a usability standpoint, it's very well instrumented, it's got very happy users, it's got an awesome growth profile, and so we should still ...
turns.zh: 最重要的经验是，所有工作都必须按部就班地推进。虽说没有理由拖延行动，但必须按顺序推进，并自下而上地领导团队。决策必须基于实际情况。我过去11个月最大的收获之一，就是更加信任自己的直觉。发现其他部门的成功模式在产品团队同样适用，但同时我也面临着挑战——因为此前从未领导过产品团队，所以必须从零开始思考每个问题。比如，我不会盲目引用网上观点或专家见解，而是会将其拆解成基本要素，再结合Rippling的实际情况进行应用。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: It's got an awesome growth profile. So we should be really focused on the adoption metrics because I think that's going to be an important ingredient to low churn over time, removing friction from the implementation process as an example. (00:25:13): There are other parts of our product where I would say I don't care at all about adoption and am much more focused on foundational things like I said earlier, test coverage or whatever, just to make sure that the thing is stable and good and delivering exactly what it's supposed to deliver once it's adopted.
turns.zh: 就拿招聘系统来说，用户体验已达标，数据指标完善，用户反馈积极，增长曲线亮眼，因此我们必须重点关注相关数据。但有些产品线，比如申请人追踪系统，虽然数据表现优异，但我并不认为所有产品都需要追踪用户采用率。关键在于，根据产品实际情况灵活应用策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now that you're on the inside of the product team, what's something that you think people outside of product, say Matt two years ago or other, I don't know, go to market leads, other execs should hear, need to understand about product that they don't until they're on the inside?
turns.zh: 现在身处产品团队，我发现很多非产品人士（比如两年前的Matt，或其他市场负责人等高管）都缺乏对产品思维的深刻理解。只有亲身经历，才能真正领会其中的奥秘。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I'll give you another framework that I like to use. In the financial world, there's this concept of alpha. Alpha is outperformance relative to the index. So that's why you have seekingalpha.com as a very popular website. What they mean by that is you're looking to buy something, some combination of assets that will outperform, let's say the S&P 500, if that's your benchmark. And they were willing to interrupt us to ask more questions," and and and, like a lot of the sort of basic human interaction models. (00:38:25): You never think that giving someone an impossible task and even including the L5 person versus the VP on the same thing would be productive. And let's just say our recruiting team still sort of kvetches a bit about this and feels like we eliminate people too aggressively at this stage of the interview process. But I've found the wisdom in it and think it's actually quite useful to give everyone the same simple, complicated prompt and just see. Hand them a drill bit, give them the concrete wall and see if they can get a millimeter or an inch into the concrete. They're never going to get all the way through the wall. It doesn't matter. You're going to learn a lot. And I've found that to be kind of an eye-opening new thing for me that has been fun. (00:39:04): Look, the joy of product and the joy of product management and the joy of being part of product, I think there's a bunch of joys actually, if I could give you a sort of running list, but one of the big joys is that you get to work with some of the smartest people in software. Engineers are very smart. They're not always the best sort of social entities. Salespeople are awesome social entities. They're not always the best systems thinkers. You go down the list. (00:39:28): But the magic of product management is that you kind of have to ... We talk about the mini CEO. I think it's kind of a stupid misnomer, but there's some wisdom there. And I think the wisdom is that you have to be a polymath. You've got to be really good at working with other people. You got to be good at communications and articulation. You got to be good at project management. You got to be good at the science and the math and the engineering. And it's really fucking cool. So I think one of the great joys of this job for me has been interacting with the tippity top of the smartest and most polymathic people in the industry. (00:40:01): I'll say one other thing about what I love about leading product, which is as a COO, my job was to accept the product as it was and optimize everything around that. My job was to make sure that the product operations, in our business, the interface to the insurance carriers, the interface to the payment entities, the government regulators, that stuff all just sort of worked. It was to make sure that our sales engine, our marketing engine, all the go to-market stuff optimized itself around what the product was. It was about recruiting and making sure we got people in to work on the product. You kind of go down any function that isn't in R&D, and I had some hand in trying to figure out how to make that function work to the best of its ability, given what the product was. (00:40:48): And now that I lead product, I'm like, "Oh, wow. This is the high order bit." Not that I didn't sort of understand that, but now I really get that product is the high order bit. If you get the product right, it fits in the market, everything else gets easier. Finance is easier, sales is easier, marketing is easier, recruiting is easier, everything gets fucking easier. So I think the other joy of leading the product function is that I get to set the highest order bit in the business's success to one.
turns.zh:
刚加入产品团队时，我接触到一种面试框架或策略——这在我的职业生涯中几乎从未使用过：每位不同级别的产品经理都会接到同一份极其困难的案例研究题目。这种案例研究要求你同时考虑多个维度，思考数据传播问题，还涉及相当深度的技术细节。（00:37:37）我们用以评估候选人表现的评分标准，旨在展现初级产品经理、资深产品经理乃至高管应具备的能力。大多数候选人完成面试后都感觉糟糕透顶，认为自己表现不佳。但在我们看来，他们中的一些人表现出色，成功捕捉到三四个关键点——尽管还有十个难点未能触及——面对质疑其解决方案的反馈时，他们不固执己见，愿意中断提问并追问更多细节，这正是基本的人际交互模式。（00:38:25）你绝不会认为给人布置不可能完成的任务——哪怕让L5级别员工和VP同坐一桌——能有成效。但我已领悟到其中的智慧：让所有人面对同样复杂的挑战，观察他们的表现，实在是很有价值。就像递给他们钻头，让他们面对混凝土墙壁，看看他们能否钻入一毫米或一英寸。即便无法完全突破，也能收获宝贵经验。这对我而言是个启发性的新体验，乐趣十足。（00:39:04）说回产品工作的乐趣所在——产品管理的快乐，产品团队的归属感……若要列举清单，实在太多了。但核心乐趣在于，你得与软件行业最聪明的人共事：工程师们极其精明，但社交能力欠佳；销售人员善于交际，却非系统思考者……诸如此类。（00:39:28）而产品管理的魔力在于，你必须……我们常说产品经理是“迷你CEO”，这或许是个不太准确的比喻，但其中蕴含着智慧：你必须是全才，善于与人合作，具备沟通表达能力，还要精通项目管理、科学与工程学。这种感觉实在酷毙了。对我而言，工作中最大的乐趣之一，就是与行业内最顶尖、最全能的产品人才互动。（00:40:01）再谈谈我热爱产品领导岗位的另一个原因：作为COO，我的职责是接纳现有产品，优化其周边生态。确保产品运营、与保险公司的接口、与支付机构的对接、政府监管等各环节无缝衔接。还要确保我们的销售引擎、营销引擎正常运转。
所有市场推广策略都是围绕产品本身进行优化的。关键在于招聘人才，确保他们能专注于产品开发。只要是研发之外的任何职能部门，我都会参与其中，尽力让这些部门在现有产品框架下发挥最大潜力。（00:40:48）如今我身为产品负责人时才意识到："天哪，这才是重中之重啊！"其实我并非不明白这一点，但现在我真正领悟到，产品才是核心要素。只要产品设计得当，市场就能顺畅接纳，剩下的一切都会变得容易许多——财务管理更得心应手，销售更游刃有余，市场营销更行云流水，招聘也更加顺畅。总之，领导产品团队最大的乐趣在于，我能为公司的成功设定最高标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really great to hear. A lot of times people outside product don't understand these sorts of things and look down on product a lot of times, especially sales folks, COOs a lot of times. I love that you're seeing this and realizing this and recognizing just how important and interesting and challenging this work is and just how awesome PMs are. As you know, a lot of people are a very anti-product manager. "Why do we need product managers? We don't need them. Slow everything down, all this process."
turns.zh: 听到你这么说真是太好了。很多产品之外的同事不理解这类事情，甚至对产品部门心存偏见，尤其是销售人员和首席运营官们。我很欣慰你能意识到这一点，认识到这份工作的重要性、趣味性和挑战性，也领悟到产品经理是多么了不起的存在。正如你所知，很多人对产品经理抱有偏见，诸如“我们为什么需要产品经理？根本不需要。他们只会拖慢进程，搞那么多流程。”

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yeah. I have a distinction there, which is that I'm anti-shitty product managers.
turns.zh: 是啊。我要强调的是，我反对的是糟糕的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly how I put it. If you hate product managers, you just haven't worked with a great product manager.
turns.zh: 我就是这么说的。如果你讨厌产品经理，那说明你没遇到过优秀的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Well, it's like, look, I love wine, wine's one of my things. And I've learned a lot about wine. And one of my favorite lines is like, "I don't like Chardonnay." And I'm like, "No, no, no, no, no. Chardonnay's are the most fucking amazing varieties of wine in the world. You just haven't had good Chardonnay. And there's a Chardonnay out there for you." Product management, it's like you don't like product management, you think product managers suck. It's like, well, you just haven't had a good Chardonnay yet.
turns.zh: 就好比，我热爱葡萄酒，这是我的爱好之一。我对葡萄酒研究颇深。我最喜欢的一句话是：“我不喜欢霞多丽。”我会说：“不不不！霞多丽可是世界上最棒的葡萄酒品种。你只是没喝过好霞多丽罢了。总有一款适合你的。” 产品管理也是如此，如果你不喜欢产品管理，觉得产品经理很烂，那就说明你还没遇到过优秀的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly what I [inaudible 00:42:24]-

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Once you have one, you can't unlearn it.
turns.zh: 一旦你遇到过，就再也忘不了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're like, "Let's find that PM ASAP."
turns.zh: 你会说：“我们得尽快找到那个产品经理。”

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: No, let's find that Chardonnay ASAP.
turns.zh: 不，我们得尽快找到那款霞多丽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:42:34] with some Chardonnay. You touched on this product market fit point, and I want to double down on this thread. You've had a couple really interesting experiences of struggling to find product market fit with your own startup. You said you worked on it for nine years, you said?
turns.zh: [00:42:34听不清]，再配上点霞多丽。你之前提到了产品市场匹配这个点，我想在此深挖一下。你在自己的创业公司寻找产品市场匹配时遇到了不少挑战，据你所说，你为此奋斗了九年？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then with Rippling, complete opposite, extreme product market fit, up and to the right. What's something you've learned about just that that you think people maybe don't understand about what it feels like, what it takes to get to product market fit, how things change?
turns.zh: 好的。然后在Rippling项目上，情况完全相反，产品市场匹配堪称完美，一切都顺风顺水。你从中领悟到了什么呢？你觉得人们可能不理解产品市场匹配的真谛，理解不到达到这种状态需要付出什么努力，以及它会带来怎样的改变？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: There's a line that this venture capitalist, whose name I will not mention, said, which was that product market fit is a sort of thing where you absolutely know it when you see it, and therefore if you don't absolutely know it, you don't have it. (00:43:17): And this kind of gets back to my point about learning from mistakes versus successes. It's like, ah, man, over and over again, over the course of the many years that I spent at Inkling, we thought we had it. We thought we had product market fit, maybe, maybe. And in hindsight, with the benefit of now having experienced solid product market fit, it was so, so obvious that we didn't. (00:43:45): And I've invested in like 60 companies or 70 companies. I don't know, it's not something I actively do. But opportunities, by virtue, I think, of my role at Rippling, sort of show up. And I talk to lots of entrepreneurs and I love it and I find it super stimulating and I love the fresh ideas and it's just something I do as a real cherry on top of the sport that I play already. But when I get the investor updates for the guys who've been at it for like three, four years and I read the updates from them that I sent to my investors in 2011 and 2012, I'm kind of heartbroken. (00:44:29): We talk in Silicon Valley about never quit, but that is complete absolute venture capital bullshit. The incentive of venture capitalist is to put money into your company and milk you dry. They never get their money back. There is no way for them to take that investment back. So the only logical desire that they would have is for you to keep trying against all odds because there is the occasional example where someone pivoted from A to X and it was wildly different and it worked. Slack was originally some sort of a gaming company and became corporate chat. Airbnb maybe. It's like there's some examples of companies having made wild pivots and succeeded, but man, is that rare. Just so exceedingly rare. (00:45:21): And I think it's important to remember, I'm 45 years old, we're going to be on the planet, the average age of a man in the United States when he dies is something in the mid 70s. I got 20, 30, maybe if I'm lucky, 40 years left on the planet. Very conscious of the time that I have. And I don't regret what I did at Inkling, I learned a lot. It informed what I do now. I don't think the chapter I'm in right now could have come without the chapters before it. So it's a beautiful, wonderful thing that I did what I did. But when I read the investor update and I'm like, "You're where I was and you are not getting out of this." (00:45:56): The Silicon Valley try until you die mindset is not pro-entrepreneur, it's pro-venture capitalist. And I know why that is, but I think it's important to say out loud that you should fucking quit. You should reset the clock, you should reset the cap table because trust me, product market fit when it arrives is insane and it's exciting and you should pursue it. And never delude yourself into believing you have it when you don't. It is dangerous and regrettable. How's that for a speech?
turns.zh: 有一位我不便透露姓名的风险投资家曾说过，产品市场契合度就是那种当你看到它时就绝对能认出来的东西。因此，如果你不确定是否具备这种契合度，那你其实就根本没有它。（00:43:17）这让我想起了我对从失败中学习与从成功中学习的看法。回想起我在Inkling工作的那些年，我们总以为自己找到了产品市场契合度，但事后看来——如今我已亲身经历过真正的产品市场契合度——很显然我们当时并没有做到。（00:43:45）我投资了大约60到70家公司。我不知道这是不是我刻意为之，但由于我在Rippling的角色，投资机会自然而然地出现。我与许多创业者交流，乐在其中，觉得这非常有启发，也喜欢新鲜的创意理念，对我而言这只是我所热爱的运动之外的额外奖励。但当我看到那些创业者历经三四年仍在苦苦挣扎的投资报告，读到我2011和2012年发给投资者的报告时，我心里总有种失落感。（00:44:29）在硅谷，我们常说永不放弃，但这完全是风险投资者的胡说八道。风险投资者的动机就是把钱投进你的公司，然后榨干你。他们永远拿不回自己的钱，也没法收回投资。因此，他们唯一的希望就是看着你不顾一切地继续尝试，因为偶尔会有人从A转向X，完全变了样却成功了。Slack最初是一家游戏公司，后来变成了企业聊天工具；Airbnb或许也是如此。确实有一些公司成功实现了彻底转型，但这种情况实在太罕见了。（00:45:21）我认为重要的是要记住，我已经45岁了，平均而言美国男性寿命在70岁左右。我还能在地球上再待20、30年，或许运气好的话还能活到40岁。我非常清楚自己的时间有限。我不后悔在Inkling的经历，我学到了很多。这些经验也影响着我现在的工作。我觉得如果没有之前的经历，我现在所处的阶段是不可能实现的。所以我做过的事确实很棒。但当我读到投资报告，看到创业者处境和我曾经一样却毫无出路时，我总会心痛不已。（00:45:56）硅谷那种不成功便成仁的心态根本不利于创业者，而只对风险投资有利。我知道其中的原因，但我认为有必要大声说出来：你他妈应该退出。重置时间表，重组股权结构，因为相信我，当产品市场契合度真正到来时，那种激动人心的感觉简直令人疯狂，你必须全力以赴去追寻它。千万别自欺欺人地以为自己已经具备了它。这既危险又令人遗憾。这算是一次演讲吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. The anti-VC speech. The-
turns.zh: 太棒了。这篇反风险投资的演讲。真-

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I got more where that came from. By the way, it's not anti-VC. It's anti-
turns.zh: 我还能讲更多类似的例子。顺便说一句，这不是反风险投资。这是反-

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 风险投资的宣传。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Everybody's acting in accordance with their incentives in Silicon Valley, the executives, the founders, the venture ... Everybody's, of course, behaving in accordance with their incentives. And the venture capitalists have very strong enduring incentives that have shaped the dynamic of how Silicon Valley works. There's nothing wrong with that. It's just really, really important to point them out and scream at them for the 25-year-old entrepreneur who has no fucking clue how this stuff works. (00:47:12): Trust me, the 45-year-old entrepreneur or the 50-year-old venture capitalist who've been in the game for a while, they get it. They've observed it. They know what it's like. The system is there to take advantage of the people who don't, or at least it is the easiest prey for the incentive structures, not for venture capitalists as individual people who are beautiful and all of them are just really wonderful people. It's just that the incentive structures lead to some real harm, I think, in certain cases.
turns.zh: 硅谷的每个人——高管、创始人、风险投资家……当然，他们都是在按照自身利益行事。而风险投资家们有着极其强大的、持久的激励机制，这些机制塑造了硅谷运作的动态模式。这本身并无过错，但对于那些对行业运作机制一无所知的25岁创业者来说，确实需要特别指出并严厉批评他们。（00:47:12）：相信我，那些已深耕行业多年的45岁或50岁创业者，他们心知肚明。他们观察过这一切，深有体会。整个系统就是为了利用那些不了解规则的人——或者至少说，它是那些激励机制最容易捕食的猎物，而非针对那些善良且出色的风险投资家个体。只是激励机制在某些情况下会带来真正的危害。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the thing I find is when you do quit, VCs ... I'm always just like, "Hey, let me know when you're starting your next thing. I'm excited to invest." They're rarely, unless they're not a great VC, rarely are they just pissed at you for how could you possibly not make this work [inaudible 00:47:52].
turns.zh: 我发现，当你真的退出（创业）时，风险投资家们……我总是会说，“嘿，等你下次创业时告诉我。我很乐意投资。”除非他们不是优秀的风险投资家，否则他们很少会因为你没能成功而生气。（00:47:52，语音不清）

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: That's the thing, as a founder, when it's time to throw in the towel on your business and you're so obsessed with giving money back to the cap table, I always remind the entrepreneur like, "Hey, if you're in the seed investing game, your forecast is zero. Your assumption on every investment is that it's going to go to zero." Any seed investor who doesn't take that stance is off their rocker anyway. They're a very bad investor. Seek investors who play the long game, who want to be in your second and third company and are willing to take a bet on the first one and let it go to zero so that you can get on with stuff. This is like, I've had that conversation many times.
turns.zh: 关键在于，作为创始人，当你不得不放弃自己的事业时，又过于执着于向投资方退款时，我总是提醒创业者：“嘿，如果你参与种子轮投资，你的预测就是零。每笔投资的假设都是它会归零。” 任何不持这种态度的种子投资人都疯了。他们是糟糕的投资者。要寻找那些能与你共度长征的投资者，他们希望参与你的第二家和第三家公司，愿意在第一家公司上押注，让它归零，这样你才能继续前行。这类对话我已经多次进行过了。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Here, look, history provides us with a clear guide. When you look at companies having hit it big, they hit big pretty quick. It's very, very dangerous to be late to the party, it's very, very dangerous to be early to the party, and the vast majority of the time, that's the problem. Rippling, had it been started in 2014, would not be what it is today. I think Rippling, had it been started today, would not be what-

(00:52:56): Well, if you recognize that the market is immutable, no amount of tweeting, LinkedIn posting, advertising is going to change whether the market wants your product. turns.zh: 是啊，对啊。我觉得这是一个被严重误解的基本逻辑。当创始人给我发消息说「嘿，帮我点赞领英帖子和推特宣传这次发布会」时，我会照做。我会转发、点赞之类的。反正也没人关注我的推特账号，所以无所谓，但我还是会做这些事。但我心里想，这根本就不是重点。这不是伟大公司的构建之道。这可能是一个引发关注的契机，但并非关键所在，因为没人真正在乎你的公司。你的发布会并不重要。就像把大石头扔进大海，相比创业公司和产品的大海而言，你的发布会不过是沧海一粟。因此，你必须脚踏实地，一砖一瓦地把公司建立起来，而这些发布会其实并没有太大意义。那么你该如何看待这一点呢？当你意识到市场是不可改变的，再多的推特宣传、领英帖子或广告都无法改变市场对你的产品的需求。它们或许能提高产品的知名度，但无法改变人们是否真的想要它。那么你就需要转换思路。你必须把你的创业公司视为在宇宙中进行的一场实验，看看能得到什么回报。用药物研发和受体结合的类比来说，基因泰克公司的科学家们从不认为他们能通过市场营销手段让药物在人体内发挥更好的效果。对那种药物的受体存在与否，市场早已给出了答案。当他们开发产品时，目标就是验证受体是否存在，但结果早已注定。对于你开发的每一个软件产品来说，市场要么会欣然接受并推广它，要么不会。不要先把产品推向市场，发现失败后再试图通过营销来扭转局面，因为受体很可能根本不存在。对我来说，这种思维方式非常解放，因为现在我只需要找到正确的解决方案，而无需再费力去说服市场为我正在开发的产品创造受体。
