turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: So you kicked this conversation off sort of invoking the extraordinary outcomes, demand, extraordinary efforts line, hat tip to Dan Gill, and these are part and parcel. Man, understanding the nature of the universe is a pretty good way to work within it, and so power law distributions happen everywhere. It explains why so few people control so much wealth. It explains why Steph Curry is just so vastly better than the next guy down on the list on the basketball team. It explains why populations are concentrated into a relatively small number of mega cities in the world. It's like, power law distribution just plays out everywhere, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. It sort of plays out in many dynamics. (01:01:47): People tend to think that the world plays on a more linear relationship where the X and Y axis are sort of Y equals X, but that is absolutely not the case, and the implications are profound. It's like if you build something to 80 or 90%, the Y axis is barely budged yet. You haven't hit the inflection point in terms of reward, and so the implication of the power law more broadly is that people who are in the top 10%, the top 5%, don't just get 10 or 20% more reward. They get 10X the reward or 100X the reward. It's really dramatic. (01:02:20): Entropy, the second law of thermodynamics is a very simple concept. It's the reason your sock drawer becomes messy. It's the reason that potholes form. It's the reason we have to put so much energy into maintaining the aircraft we fly to keep them safe because they really, really, really want to fall apart, and that's the nature of things. If you abandon a city for a few months, it starts to go fallow, and so entropy is just this concept that shit tends toward disorder. (01:02:48): The universe, I mean, life itself is a temporary victory against entropy. You and I should not exist. The sun gives energy to the planet. It organizes stuff that we can eat and we fight entropy until we lose the battle somewhere, as I said earlier at the age of 70 or 80, if we're lucky. What does this have to do with product? This is really about effort. (01:03:17): The only antidote to entropy, the only antidote to decay in a system is energy. You got to inject energy. So if you have a code base, every line of code that you add to that code base increases the entropy of that system and demands ever more energy from human beings to go and intend to it to make sure it doesn't break, and if you want to achieve greatness, if you want an extraordinary outcome, and in particular, if you want to be in the top 10%, top 5% on the X axis so that the Y axis is through the roof, then you have to relentlessly inject energy at every single step of the game. Teams will, sadly, but because we are all human, teams will always optimize for local comfort over company outcomes. (01:04:11): Not because they get together and think, "We should do that," although unions do do that unequivocally, deliberately, but even in a collection of product managers or engineers, what's going to happen over time is entropy is going to creep in and people are going to optimize for local comfort. Your job as an executive, as a leader, is to fight that entropy tooth and nail every single day. It means that every time you see a bug, every time you see a bug, not most of the time, every time you go and you drop it at the feet of the product manager or the engineering manager, every time, in public, preferably, it means that every time someone comes to you to hire someone and says that they have skipped the back channel, every time you're like, "You can't hire this person unless you do the back channel," it means that when you get into the board and tired zone on any process, that you as the executive have got to demand the 99th percentile of energy, because otherwise entropy creeps in and the system decays. You have to do this. (01:05:19): One of the messages that I delivered recently at our big executive big... Like our top 75 manager offsite that we do roughly every 18 months, was a reminder that if the purest form of ambition and the purest and most intense source of energy in the business is the founder CEO, that every next concentric circle of management beyond the founder CEO has the potential to be an order of magnitude drop off in intensity, and that is dangerous because if you go to two layers and it's two orders of magnitude drop off and signal and intensity, that is a very dysfunctional organization. So what I say to the team was, it's not that you need to buffer people from the intensity of the CEO, it's that you need to absolutely mirror that intensity. (01:06:13): There are plenty of constituents in the business around you who will advocate for relaxing. There is an infinite supply of people under you who will buffer other team members from the intensity of the demands. Your job is not to be one of those buffers. Your job is to preserve that intensity at its highest possible level and let the buffering happen somewhere else, and that's the point is that entropy creeps into the system insidiously and slowly over time off your radar and you have to maintain that intensity every minute of every day to try and fight it if you want to stay at the extreme right end of the power law that obviously governs the outcome of everything that we build.
turns.zh:
接下来，你开启了这场对话，提到了"非凡的成果、需求、非凡的努力"等概念，这里要特别感谢丹·吉尔（Dan Gill），这些都是密不可分的。理解宇宙的本质是顺应其规律的绝佳方式，因此幂律分布无处不在。它解释了为何少数人能掌控巨额财富，解释了为何斯蒂芬·库里（Steph Curry）在篮球队中远超其他球员的表现，也解释了为何全球人口集中在少数特大城市。幂律分布无处不在，一旦你领悟了这一点，就再也无法忽视它。它在诸多动态中发挥作用。

（01:01:47）：人们往往认为世界遵循线性关系，X轴和Y轴的关系是Y=X，但事实绝非如此。其深层含义意义重大。即使你将某个项目推进到80%或90%，Y轴几乎毫无波动。这意味着你尚未触及回报的拐点，更广泛而言，处于前10%或前5%的群体获得的回报并非10%或20%，而是10倍或100倍的回报。这差异巨大，令人震惊。

（01:02:20）：熵，热力学第二定律是一个非常简单的概念。它解释了为什么你的袜子抽屉会变得凌乱，为什么道路会出现坑洼。它解释了为什么我们必须投入大量精力维护飞机安全，因为飞机真的非常非常想解体，这就是事物的本质。如果你放弃一座城市几个月，它就会荒废。所以熵就是事物趋于无序的概念。

（01:02:48）：宇宙，准确来说生命本身，就是对熵的暂时胜利。你我本不该存在。太阳为地球提供能量，组织出我们可食用的物质。我们与熵抗争，直到七八十岁时输掉这场战斗。那么这与产品有什么关系？关键在于努力。

（01:03:17）：对抗熵、对抗系统衰败的唯一解药就是能量。你必须注入能量。因此，增加代码库的每一行代码都会增加系统的熵，迫使人类投入更多精力去维护，确保其不崩溃。若想达成卓越成果，特别是跻身前10%或前5%行列，让Y轴直线攀升，那么你必须在每一步都全力注入能量。遗憾的是，团队会因人性而优化本地舒适度而非公司成果。

（01:04:11）：这并非因为他们坐下来商量"我们应该这么做"（尽管工会确实会刻意这么做），但即便在产品经理或工程师团队中，熵也会逐渐侵蚀，人们也会优先优化本地舒适度。而作为高管和领导者，你的职责就是日复一日与熵抗争到底。这意味着每次你发现漏洞时，每次你发现漏洞（不是大多数情况，而是每次），当你把问题推给产品经理或工程经理时，每次，当有人私下找你招聘却跳过正常渠道时，你都要公开质问。
除非你能另辟蹊径，否则你就无法招到这个人。  
这意味着，当你在任何流程中陷入停滞和疲惫的阶段时，作为高管，你必须调动出99%的能量，否则熵会悄然侵蚀，系统就会崩溃。你必须做到这一点。  
（01:05:19）：最近我在一次大型高管会议上传达的信息……比如我们大约每18个月举办一次的75位高管离职会议，就是要提醒大家，如果企业中最纯粹的雄心和最强烈的能量源泉是创始人兼CEO，那么在创始人CEO之外的每一层管理层，其能量强度都可能呈指数级衰减。这很危险，因为如果下两层管理层的能量强度和信号强度都下降两个量级，那这个组织就严重失灵了。  
所以我对团队说：你不需要让员工远离CEO的强压环境，而是要完全匹配这种强压力。  
（01:06:13）：你身边有很多下属会主张降低标准。你的下属中永远有无穷无尽的人会为其他团队成员减弱压力。你的职责不是充当这种缓冲者，而是要将这种强压力保持在最高水平，让缓冲工作由其他人来完成。关键在于熵会逐渐潜入系统，在你察觉不到的情况下慢慢侵蚀。若想保持在权力法则的极右端，你必须每时每刻都保持这种强压力，与熵抗争到底。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does that look like to pass along that intensity? What does that feel like? What does that look like? So say Parker comes to you, "This bug sucks. I got this broken screen." You cut off your finger. Maybe that's the example. (01:07:18): Okay. Still got them. I got all 10.
turns.zh: 怎样才能传递出那种强烈的紧迫感？那会是怎样的感觉？具体又该怎么做呢？比如说帕克来找你说：“这破手机太烦人了，屏幕都坏了。”你直接截掉自己的手指。这或许就是个例子。（01:07:18）好的，我现在还是能想到10个例子。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I'll give you concrete examples. Actually, the joke that I sort of played on this one when I presented to the team was that the next sort of slide in my presentation was with the sound effect, the Slack huddle thing, and Parker's icon in Slack is just, he uses the generic yellow...
turns.zh: 我会给你们举具体的例子。实际上，我给团队做演示时开的一个玩笑是，接下来的一张幻灯片配上了Slack上的群组通知音效，而帕克在Slack里的头像用的是默认的黄色鸡蛋图标……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The egg?
turns.zh: 那个鸡蛋？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: It's funny, and so everybody knows the yellow egg is Parker, and so the next slide in the presentation was boop, boop, boop, boop, boop, boop, boop, which is the sound that Slack makes when someone calls you, and it was Parker Conrad is inviting you to a huddle, and then the next slide was Parker Conrad is modeling personal intensity, and the idea is that if you know, you know, if you've ever been dragged into an... "I want to talk about this fucking problem right now and whatever you're doing, unless it's an interview, I want you to come and have a conversation with me." (01:08:13): That intensity is one place where it plays out. Every product team at Rippling, and we have a lot of them now, have public feedback channels. I am in there upside down on everything I find when I use those products, and I just model for everybody that this is how at least I want to do it, which is, "I don't like this. I don't understand this. Tell me why this is this way." Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, and people jump in and respond. The factory inspection process that I mentioned, which is where at the end of the assembly line, I jump out with the pickle and we talk about all of the elements. You have to record a loom of every major flow through the product. I personally review every one of those flows, I got a backlog I got to catch up on today and provide feedback to people always in a public channel so that every other product manager and engineering manager can jump in and see how the process has worked for other teams. (01:09:01): It's about modeling the intensity publicly so that other people can say, "Okay, this is how we do things around here," and it gives the reaction from the team that received the message that you have to inject that energy every minute of every day and that there are no exceptions, was not like, "Ooh, that's exhausting." The reaction is, "Oh, that is so invigorating." It's so wonderful to hear that we're going to achieve these great outcomes, or at least we have a shot at doing so, and that you're empowering me to follow my instinct, which is to really push for the best result. (01:09:39): The reaction universally is like, "Ugh, what a relief that I get to go be intense," because nobody in a position of leadership wants to be chill, and what's worse than a chill boss? No, don't work for a chill boss. Don't be a chill boss. It's the most pejorative label I could give you. Chill boss or chill PM. Don't be chill. Chill doesn't accomplish shit. Be intense. Be good, be respectful, be intense. Don't be chill.
turns.zh: 这挺有趣的，大家都知道黄色鸡蛋代表帕克。所以演示中的下一张幻灯片会发出提示音，显示Slack的群组通知，然后出现帕克·康拉德邀请你参加会议的通知，再下一张幻灯片是帕克·康拉德展示个人紧迫感的场景。关键是，如果你懂的话，你就会明白，某个产品经理突然把你拉进会议室，说：“我现在就要讨论这个破问题，不管你在做什么，除非是采访，否则你必须来和我聊聊。”（01:08:13）这种紧迫感在Rippling的每个产品团队中都有体现。我们现在有很多产品团队，都设有公开反馈渠道。我会不遗余力地在这些产品中发现任何问题，并向大家展示我希望如何处理这些问题：“我不喜欢这样。我不明白为什么要这样。告诉我为什么要这样做。”轰轰轰轰轰轰，人们会积极响应。我提到的工厂检查流程，就是在装配线末端，我带着黄瓜去检查所有流程环节。每个主要流程我都会亲自审核，今天我还有积压的任务要处理，并在公开渠道上提供反馈，这样其他产品经理和工程经理就能参与进来，看看其他团队的流程是如何运作的。（01:09:01）关键在于公开传递这种紧迫感，让其他人能说：“好吧，这就是我们这里的做事方式。”团队得到的反馈是：“哦，太棒了，这太振奋人心了。” 听到我们将达成这些伟大成果，或者至少有机会做到时，那种兴奋感真是太好了。而且你赋予我追随直觉的权力，那就是真正争取最佳结果。（01:09:39）普遍的反应都是：“啊，总算能放松一下了。” 因为没有哪个领导者愿意保持冷淡，而比冷淡的老板更糟糕的是什么？不，别为冷淡的老板工作，也别当冷淡的老板。这是我能给出的最贬义的标签了。冷淡的老板或者冷淡的产品经理。别冷淡。冷淡解决不了任何问题。要充满紧迫感。要优秀，要尊重他人，要充满紧迫感。别冷淡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Again, this advice comes from where we started, which is this is what success looks like, because somebody that is less chill than you is going to find that crack and come after your market. Is that the gist?
turns.zh: 再次说明，这条建议源于我们的初衷：成功的模样往往就是如此，因为那些比你更拼命的人会发现你的弱点并抢占你的市场份额。是这个意思吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: For sure. I mean, again, if you're chill and you move the X axis down 10 or 20 points, the Y axis collapses. It doesn't just drop 10 or 20%. The Y axis collapses, and this is just kind of true in everything we do. So yeah, if you want to win, you should probably try.
turns.zh: 确实如此。我的意思是，如果你太佛系，把X轴降低10或20个点，Y轴就会崩盘。它不会只下降10或20%。Y轴会彻底崩盘，这在我们做任何事情上都是如此。所以没错，如果你想赢，那你或许应该尝试拼一把。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is what I always say to people trying to build lifestyle businesses. There's always this idea, "I'm going to build a side business, I'm going to make recurring income, it's going to be amazing," and in my experience, anytime there's a market or something shows up that's juicy and there's ways to make money, somebody's going to come at you and work harder, raise more money, and there's only so long you can maintain that.
turns.zh: 这就是我对那些想打造生活方式型企业的创业者常说的话。总有人抱着这样的想法：“我要做个副业，赚点持续收入，那样就完美了。” 但以我的经验来看，只要市场上出现诱人机遇，赚钱的机会一来，就总会有人比你更拼命、筹集更多资金，而你能维持这种局面的时间终究是有限的。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Well, man, there's a whole other podcast episode on the concept of leverage. If you sell your time, you've only got 24 hours a day to give, but if you can create a product that scales, the marginal cost of a unit of that product is zero like software, it's going to be competitive, man. Sell your time, it's not going to be super competitive, but achieve that level of leverage and it's a pretty efficient market.
turns.zh: 兄弟，关于杠杆效应的概念，我们可以专门做一期播客来探讨。如果你靠出卖时间赚钱，一天就24小时可供交易，但如果你能开发出可规模化的产品，比如软件之类的，边际成本为零，那竞争力就强多了。出卖时间的竞争力终究有限，但达到那种杠杆效应，市场效率就会大大提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To close out this thread of intensity and adding energy to everything, something I've heard about you is you're big on escalating. You're a big fan of escalating issues, and also you always tell people to never not give you negative feedback, to always share feedback to not hide anything. Tell me about those two.
turns.zh: 最后聊聊激情和注入能量的话题。我听说你特别强调不断提升标准。你热衷于把问题升级处理，还总鼓励别人别藏着掖着，要勇于分享负面反馈。这两点能详细说说吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Fundamentally, the most selfish thing you can do is withhold feedback from someone. Who are you optimizing for when you do that? What are you optimizing for when you think a thought that would help someone improve and you avoid giving it to them because it would make you uncomfortable? Well, you're optimizing for your own comfort and it's fundamentally selfish. It's the most selfish thing you could possibly do, is withhold feedback that would otherwise be useful to someone because you don't want to be uncomfortable. Well, that's not how high performance teams operate. So I demand feedback, and I give it, and it doesn't mean that when I give feedback, it's not open to being questioned or discussed. I mean, of course it is, but when I observe something, I try to say it. That's the feedback topic. (01:12:35): The part of this that has been interesting to me is that people withhold, escalate, the customers withhold. Customers don't want to escalate to me as an executive. Even the founders in whose businesses I've invested who use Rippling are reluctant to hit me up when something goes wrong because they don't want to bother me, but it's literally my job, literally my job to find things, problems, and make them better, and by virtue of making those specific things better, to iterate on the processes so that the system that builds the system can get better. (01:13:09): There's no greater gift to me as a product executive than receiving an escalation from a customer. We have an escalations team at Rippling, which sounds weird, but it's people who are just particularly skilled at pistol whipping other people in the company to get to real root causes, real root causes. Not like throw away the word root cause, like, "Oh, we fixed the data error and shut the ticket down." No, you went and you found the software that created the data error, and then you found the system that created the software that created the data error, and you solved all of that back to the top. (01:13:44): Escalation seems extremely good at that at Rippling. So we have sort of a dedicated little team that does this for us. Escalations are a gift, and it's like, if you're a listener right now on this podcast and you are a Rippling customer and you have shit that you think we should know, the fact that I might already know it is not a reason for you to withhold the gift of your feedback. So it's an attitude that I take to this every day. I've got a little cue of some stuff that I've... Minor things that are from the last couple of days from people who had some knits and issues that I'm just like, I've got them queued up on my to do list today and I'm going to take them to the product teams directly and be like, "I'd like to understand what happened here." Not in a negative way. I just think we'll all get better if we study this one, and so yeah, escalations are a gift, feedback like that is a gift, and nobody is ever inconveniencing me when they do it.
turns.zh: 归根结底，你能做的最自私的事就是不给别人反馈。当你这么做时，你到底是在为谁优化？当你想到一个能帮助别人提升的想法，却因为觉得不舒服而避免告诉他们时，你又在为谁优化？说白了，就是为了自己的舒适感，这才是最自私的做法。正是因为不想感到不适，你才会隐瞒本可以对别人有用的反馈。高效团队可不是这样运作的。所以我要求反馈，也给予反馈，但这并不意味着我给出的反馈不能被质疑或讨论。当然可以，但当我观察到问题时，我会努力说出来。反馈就是这样一个话题。（01:12:35）让我感兴趣的是，有人隐瞒问题，客户也会隐瞒。客户不愿意向我这个高管汇报问题。即使是我投资的那些使用Rippling的创始人，也不愿意在我遇到问题时联系我，因为他们不想麻烦我，但这恰恰是我的职责——找出问题，改进流程，让构建系统的系统本身也能不断优化。（01:13:09）对我来说，作为产品高管，最大的礼物就是收到客户的反馈。我们在Rippling有一个专门的反馈团队，听起来可能有点奇怪，但他们非常善于推动公司内部人员直击问题的根源。不是那种敷衍了事，比如“哦，我们修复了数据错误，就关闭了工单”。不，你要去找到产生数据错误的软件，再找到生成这个软件的系统，然后从头到尾解决所有问题。（01:13:44）Rippling在这方面做得非常出色。因此，我们专门组建了一个小团队来负责这项工作。反馈是一份礼物。听众们，如果你是Rippling的客户，发现了我们应该知道的问题，仅仅因为我可能已经知道了，就不要因此隐瞒反馈。这是我每天秉持的态度。我收集了一些最近几天收到的反馈，来自那些遇到问题的人。我已经把它们列入了今天的待办事项清单，将直接向产品团队汇报，问他们：“我想了解这里发生了什么。”不是带着负面情绪，而是我认为只要我们研究这些问题，我们都会有所收获。所以反馈是礼物，像这样的反馈也是礼物，当人们提供反馈时，绝不会给我带来不便。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people that are listening to this and feeling like, "Man, this is so stressful and intense and just like, I don't know if I want to work this way," give them a sense of just how successful Rippling is. I think a lot of people may not even have heard of Rippling. A lot of people are like, "Yeah, it's doing great." What are some things you can share that are public or not public that give people a sense of just how massive this business has become?
turns.zh: 对于那些听了这段话后觉得“天啊，这太有压力、太紧张了，我不知道自己是否想这样工作”的人，要让他们了解Rippling取得了多大的成功。我想很多人可能甚至没听说过Rippling。很多人会说：“是啊，它发展得很棒。” 你能否分享一些公开或非公开的信息，让人们感受到这家公司已经发展得多么壮大了？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: People look at Rippling from the outside, I think they think of us as payroll and HR or whatever, which is cool. It's a bit like saying Microsoft is a desktop operating system company or it's like every company starts from somewhere.
turns.zh: 人们从外部看待Rippling时，我觉得他们可能认为我们就是做薪资和人力资源管理之类的，这挺酷的。这有点像说微软是一家桌面操作系统公司，或者说每家公司都是从某个起点起步的。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: ... system company or ... It's like every company starts from somewhere and grows out from there. We see ourselves as building the most successful business software platform in history. In fact, that's the mission statement of our product organization under the umbrella of the mission statement of the company, which is to free smart people to work on hard problems. And when you translate that from where we are today to where we think we're taking things, it's like we really do believe that the core of every workflow and everything that a company has to do, be it AI or manual traditional GUI based software, is who's doing stuff, who owns it, who's accountable? And so the people record is a really important component of that. You can argue that the customer record's also very important. And of course some big businesses have been built on that primitive as well, but we think the people primitive is actually much more important. (01:15:43): And that the only thing that hasn't been done here is somebody hasn't been ambitious enough to build a good business on top of that primitive. Workday is terrible software. Everybody agrees on that. I think Workday agrees on that. Good luck to them. But they have failed actually, despite their success, to build a really broad general purpose software platform for business software on the foundation of the people primitive. So we're going to do that. (01:16:03): And we're successful because we deliver on that promise at the scale we're at today. The fact that you can do ... and this is not a sales pitch or sort of like an advertisement for Rippling. I just think it's important to sort of contemplate that when you bring together a bunch of disparate business processes into one system on a common business data graph, an object graph, a data lake with a consistent interface, you can do some pretty magical things. (01:16:27): So we do payroll, we do HCM, we do IT, we do spend. We are about to launch a new product in the category of business intelligence and data management. And there's a whole bunch of other stuff coming beyond that. And then you layer in AI on top of this, where we alone, where we alone have all of your business data organized into this nice, neat package with a beautiful semantic layer on top of it. The AI can work magic. And we have shipped nothing, nothing yet in this category that I would say gets anywhere near what we're going to show next year. And it is going to set the standard. It is going to be the most ... The back flips that the AI is doing reading and writing data for the user just on our internal use cases at Rippling is jaw dropping. So I'm super excited about the tailwind this is going to create for us. (01:17:20): You ask about what can I share about the success of the company? What I can say, there are tens of thousands of companies that now run on Rippling. We're less than 1% of the market. And the market cap at 16 billion, I think now undervalues where we are from a revenue perspective by a long shot. There is just so much upside to do what we're doing. And SaaS might be dead-ish in terms of point solutions, but long live SaaS in terms of what we're building.
turns.zh:
……系统公司，或者……每家公司都是从某个起点起步，然后逐步发展。我们将自己视为打造史上最成功的商业软件平台。事实上，这是我们产品组织在公司使命宣言框架下的使命宣言——即解放聪明人才，让他们专注于解决难题。当我们将现状与未来愿景相比较时，我们深信每个工作流程的核心，以及企业需要完成的每一项任务，无论是人工智能还是传统基于GUI的软件，都离不开“谁在执行任务？谁是负责人？谁要承担责任？”这三个核心问题。因此，人力资源记录是至关重要的组成部分。你可以说客户记录也非常重要。当然，一些大型企业也是基于这种原始功能建立起来的，但我们认为人力资源记录的价值远远更高。
（01:15:43）：目前唯一的遗憾是，没有足够雄心壮志的人在此基础上构建出优秀的商业软件平台。Workday的软件很糟糕，这点大家都认同。我想Workday自己也承认这一点。祝他们好运吧。但尽管他们取得了成功，却未能在人力资源记录这一基础上构建出真正通用的商业软件平台。因此我们要亲自来做这件事。
（01:16:03）：我们的成功源于我们能兑现当下所处规模的承诺。事实上，你可以……这不是推销Rippling的产品，也不是广告。我只是觉得，当你将一系列不同的业务流程整合到一个基于通用业务数据图、对象图、数据湖的系统中，并赋予其统一的接口时，你能创造出令人惊叹的成果。
（01:16:27）：我们做薪资、人力资本管理、IT、支出管理等业务。即将推出商业智能和数据管理类新产品。此外还有更多创新成果。再叠加人工智能技术，我们独自将所有业务数据整理成精心打包的数据集，构建起完善的语义层。人工智能在读取和写入用户数据方面所展现的能力令人惊叹。这将为我们创造巨大的增长势头。
（01:17:20）：你问我能分享些公司成功案例吗？可以透露的是，目前数万家公司在使用Rippling。我们在市场上的份额不到1%。而160亿美元的市值估值，从营收角度看，显然低估了我们的实际价值。我们的前景广阔无比。SaaS作为点解决方案或许已近黄昏，但我们打造的SaaS生态却前景无限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me follow that thread in AI. There's been a lot of talk about AI is going to replace SaaS, as you maybe just said.
turns.zh: 让我来谈谈人工智能领域的趋势。正如你刚刚提到的，很多人都在讨论人工智能将取代SaaS服务。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yeah. People are going to vibe code their way to their payroll system, which I ... good luck to the employees of those companies.
turns.zh: 是啊。但人们会自欺欺人地以为能用代码直接替代他们的薪资系统，对此我只能说——祝那些公司的员工好运吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so what I'm hearing here is that you actually do believe a lot of SaaS companies that are selling individual solutions are in big trouble. The answer implied here is this kind of compound startup idea of you need to do a lot of things for people for them to continue to pay for your software. Is that the gist?
turns.zh: 所以我听你说，你确实认为许多销售单一解决方案的SaaS公司正面临巨大挑战。这里隐含的观点是，要让用户持续为你的软件付费，就必须为他们提供大量服务。这是关键点吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: No. I think the gist is ... there's a really good quote. I forget who it's attributable to, but it's, "There's two ways to make money in software, bundling and unbundling." And you just got to get the timing right. So this is a period of bundling. So here's the problem; point solutions don't have enough data in the age of AI to be useful. You got to be able to provide the AI with a lot of context about a lot of data so it can do things. It can do joins. It can do correlations. (01:18:49): And so if you're a point solution, you're in hard water because you've got to now rely on data from other sources. You've got to integrate to third party systems. And when you integrate to a third party system, even the best ones are still sort of drinking their data through a straw, which is a real problem. I mean, the biggest HCM software company you can think of integrates to the other biggest payroll software company you can think of through flat files via SFTP. What are they going to do? What are they going to do? It's just never going to work. It's just no way. And so I literally have no idea what they're going to do. They're just not going to build AI software, I guess. Point SaaS is sort of in a rough spot, especially when you cleave two really important systems apart and say they have to integrate. It's very, very hard. (01:19:39): The other thing that I would say about the world of, even just like not SaaS, but AI software is that point solutions in the AI world are also in a rough spot for the same reason. It's like if you're selling the shovels like OpenAI and Google with Gemini, you can make money. And if you own the mine, like Rippling, with the data, you can make money. If you're somewhere in the middle, building AI software that then tries to use the shovels from the shovel provider, but then also needs to rent out the mine, or get the ore out of somebody else's mind and start refining it, you're in a very difficult place from an economic standpoint. Because you're not going to be permitted by either of those parties to build a big business on their backs. (01:20:25): That's just not how it's going to work. They're going to demand value capture that crushes your unit economics. So I look at the landscape of AI companies that I've seen and I think you have to have a really durable, interesting insight that gives you a shot at viable unit economics to be an interesting business. And that is going to kill off 80 or 90% of the stuff that I see right now as standalone AI businesses.
turns.zh: 不。我认为关键点是……有一句很棒的名言，我忘了出自谁之口，但原意是：“在软件领域，赚钱有两种方式——打包和拆分。”关键在于把握时机。当前正处于打包阶段。问题在于：在人工智能时代，点解决方案缺乏足够的数据支持，难以发挥作用。你必须为AI提供大量数据背景，才能让它进行关联分析、数据整合等操作。（01:18:49）如果你是点解决方案提供商，就会陷入困境，因为你不得不依赖其他数据源，集成第三方系统。即便是最出色的第三方系统，也不过是通过SFTP协议从其他平台获取数据。这根本行不通。根本没戏。所以我真不知道他们会怎么做。我猜他们可能不会开发AI软件。点式SaaS正深陷困境，尤其是当你把两个关键系统割裂开，强制要求它们集成时。经济上这太难了。（01:19:39）再说人工智能软件领域，即便不谈SaaS单独看，点解决方案也面临同样的挑战。比如OpenAI和Google通过Gemini提供的挖矿工具，你能赚钱。Rippling这样的公司拥有数据矿藏，也能赚钱。但如果你处在中间位置，既要使用挖矿工具，又要从他人那里租用矿藏、提取数据进行精加工，从经济角度看就非常困难了。因为双方都不会允许你基于他们的资源建立大规模业务。这根本行不通。他们会要求分成机制，压垮你的单位经济效益。所以观察人工智能公司时，我发现必须有真正持久、有趣的洞察力，才能在单位经济效益上站稳脚跟。这意味着现在市面上80%到90%的独立AI初创公司都注定失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing here ... I love that you correct me when I get these things wrong, and that's exactly what I want. What I'm hearing is it's less about how difficult it is to build the SaaS product. It's about, do you have first party data that allows you to build an incredible AI product on top of what you've got?
turns.zh: 好的，我现在听到的是……我很高兴你能纠正我的错误，这正是我所希望的。我理解的重点不在于开发SaaS产品有多难，而是你们是否拥有第一方数据，能否在现有基础上打造出卓越的AI产品？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yep. Because look, SaaS software is a bit flipping. All SaaS software applications are bit flippers. It's an interface changing-
turns.zh: 没错。看吧，SaaS软件本质上就是在处理比特。所有SaaS应用程序都是比特操控者。这是一个界面变更——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your database?
turns.zh: 你的数据库？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yeah. Changing values in your database, that's what it does. It's a really hard problem. One of Rippling's superpowers is we're a coin sorter. You dump $20,000 for an employee in the top of the coin sorter, and it figures out what goes to the government, what goes to health insurance, what goes to your 401k, what goes to you. And it has to move all that money very, very reliably and seamlessly, very challenging software to build and manage. What's it doing? Even that is just flipping bits in a database. And so AI is a new way to flip bits. AI is just a new way to flip bits. Hopefully a way that abstracts us a little bit further from having to think because our future is Wally. It's going to be great.
turns.zh: 是的。在你的数据库中更改值，这就是它做的。这确实是个难题。Rippling的核心优势之一是我们像硬币分拣机一样运作。你把员工的2万美元工资投入硬币分拣机顶部，它就能分出该交给政府的部分、医疗保险部分、401(k)计划部分，以及属于员工的部分。它必须极其可靠、无缝地转移所有这些资金，开发和管理这样的软件极具挑战性。它在做什么？即便如此，这也只是在数据库中翻转比特。而AI是翻转比特的新方式。AI只是一种翻转比特的新方法。希望它能让我们进一步摆脱繁琐的思考，因为我们的未来是Wally。它会很棒的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of Wally, actually, I have this Matic Robot. You have one of these?
turns.zh: 说到Wally，实际上我有这个Matic机器人。你有这样的机器人吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Uh-huh.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. It's like a self-driving car robot, basically, a self-driving car. People built this robot that cleans your house. Maybe I didn't mention that. It's like a house cleaning robot that just goes around.
turns.zh: 没有。它基本上就像自动驾驶汽车机器人，就是自动驾驶汽车。人们制造了这种能清洁房屋的机器人。也许我没提到过。这就像一个只到处转悠的家用清洁机器人。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Oh, okay.
turns.zh: 哦，好的

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like a Roomba. You should have one. They're expensive, but incredibly cool. And actually in Wally, there's a scene where they actually have basically what these things look like. So it's not so far-fetched for that movie.
turns.zh: 就像Roomba机器人。你应该买一个。虽然很贵，但真的很酷。实际上在Wally里，有个场景里他们用的机器人看起来就和这些差不多。所以这在电影里并不算太牵强。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I definitely was actually quite prescient, perhaps with the exception of the gravity defying day beds.
turns.zh: 我确实挺有先见之明的，除了那些能违抗重力的大床之外。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I don't know, but that's not good news. You've seen that movie. Oh, man. So on this AI stuff, which I'm hearing is we're going to see a lot more consolidation where these point solution companies realize they need this data. This is existential, and they're going to combine and merge and bundle, as you described?
turns.zh: 是啊。我不知道，但这可不是个好消息。你看过那部电影吧。天哪。所以说AI这块，我听说我们会看到更多整合，点解决方案公司意识到他们需要这些数据。这是关乎生死存亡的，他们会像你描述的那样合并、收购、打包吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: It's possible.
turns.zh: 有可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or for now.
turns.zh: 暂且先说这些吧。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I am not an investigator on this stuff. I think there's some really interesting investors out there who I think are thinking quite deeply about this. And in particular, the conviction, which is like Mike Fornell and Sarah Guo. I think those are two investors who are hyper focused on AI. And when they made the decision to take that approach, at the time I thought that's kind of narrow. Now I'm like, no, no, no, that was the right move. And it just means that they have a very deep, deep, deep set of hypotheses that they've formed over the course of seeing every AI deal in the valley. And there are better people to ask this question of than I am. And I think if you're an entrepreneur, I recommend them to you because I think they're really smart.
turns.zh: 我并非这方面的研究者。倒是觉得有一些非常有趣的投资者，他们对此思考得非常深入。比如迈克·福内尔（Mike Fornell）和萨拉·郭（Sarah Guo），他们就专注于人工智能领域。当他们决定采取这种策略时，我当时觉得这有点狭隘。现在看来，这个决定是正确的。这意味着，他们通过在硅谷观察每一笔人工智能交易，形成了极其深刻、透彻的洞见。关于这个问题，最该请教的人不是我。如果你是一位创业者，我推荐你去找他们，因为他们确实非常聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I love those guys. Also, Sarah and Elad have a podcast called No Priors that I'd also recommend. We'll point it to you in the show notes. So on this AI note, I guess is there anything else that you think would be really helpful for founders that are working in this space building an AI startup to hear they think you were seeing of like, here's what you need to do to win in an AI company?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很欣赏这两位。此外，萨拉和埃拉德（Elad）还有一档名为《No Priors》的播客，我也推荐大家收听。我们会在节目笔记中附上链接。回到人工智能这个话题，我想有没有什么建议对正在这个领域创业、打造人工智能初创公司的创始人特别有帮助？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: So much. I actually think that if I were to give you an answer to this question right now, it would be bullshit. Yeah. I don't have anything ... Back to my point earlier, I don't have enough relevant experience in the abstract to dole out on a podcast on that topic, but I wish them luck.
turns.zh: 太多了。说实话，如果我现在要回答这个问题，肯定都是胡说八道。是的，我没有任何相关经验……回到我之前的观点，关于这个话题，我没有足够的抽象经验可以在播客上分享，但祝他们好运。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Circling back to your advice, don't ask for advice, ask for a relevant experience. And I love that that's where your mind immediately went. I'm going to take us to AI Quarter, which is a recurring segment on this podcast. And the question is just what's one way you've found AI to be useful in your work day-to-day? Is there something that you found it unlocked in how you work?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你的建议。别去寻求建议，先去寻求相关经验。这正是你第一时间想到的。接下来我们将进入《AI Quarter》环节，这是本播客的固定栏目。问题是，在日常工作中，你发现AI有何实用之处？有没有什么方面让你的工作方式焕然一新？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I mean, it's not a super exciting thing, but I'll say where I use ... So one of the most important functions that I perform as an executive is the synthesis of ideas, and the ability to communicate those ideas very clearly to people. So when I talk about the product quality list and the pickle, as something that we've come up with internally, I do turn to AI, ChatGPT and Gemini, where I take a really, let's say, angular view of some topic and I give ... really, I write the essay for the AI and I'm like, "Look, this is the crisp idea I want to communicate. Help me come up with pithy ways to articulate these things." And 80% of what it outputs is trash. It's just sort of middle of the road, average, low alpha junk. (01:25:24): But it is a thought partner, a non-judgemental thought partner where in 20% of the stuff it comes out with, I'm like, yeah, it's pretty good. That's a new word I didn't think of. That does kind of hit the nail on the head for this concept. And so if I believe that my job is to sort of bring brains along on the journey for some sort of change that I'm trying to bring about, then the most important tool is language. And I do find that the ChatGPT and Gemini do a great job of helping me refine how to articulate the concepts that I want to articulate. They are not useful in coming up with the ideas themselves.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这并非特别令人兴奋的事，但我还是要说一下我如何使用……作为高管，我最重要的职责之一是整合各种想法，并清晰地向他人传达这些想法。比如，当我谈到产品质量清单和pickle（注：可能指某种内部开发的工具）时，我确实会借助ChatGPT和Gemini。我会对某个话题提出非常尖锐的观点，然后让AI为我写一篇文章，接着我会说：“看，这就是我想传达的清晰观点。”但80%输出的内容都是垃圾。只是中规中矩、平庸、低价值的产物。（01:25:24）不过它确实是一个思想伙伴，一个不带偏见的思想伙伴。在它输出的20%内容中，我会觉得不错。这是新词汇，我之前从未想到过。它确实精准地抓住了这个概念的核心。所以，如果我认为自己的职责是带领大家共同推动变革，那么最重要的工具就是语言。我发现ChatGPT和Gemini在帮助我精确传达我想传达的概念方面做得很棒。但它们在产生创意本身方面并无帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome tip. I don't know if you've played with Claude much, but I actually find Claude is better at writing and words and language.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我不知道你有没有经常使用Claude，但我发现它在写作、用词和语言表达方面确实更出色。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: I have not spent a lot of time with Claude. I have used it, but by virtue of this conversation, I'll probably go give it a go.
turns.zh: 我没怎么深入使用Claude。不过通过这次对话，我可能会去试试看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Yeah. They're all great, but there's something about Claude that is just at writing specifically is much better, but they're all getting better all the time. There's always something new. (01:26:23): Matt, we've covered so much ground. We've touched on everything I was hoping to touch on. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you were hoping to share or anything else you wanted to touch on or leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 对呀。它们都很棒，但Claude在写作方面的表现确实更出色。不过所有产品都在不断进步，总有新东西值得期待。（01:26:23）马特，我们已经聊了很多内容，几乎涵盖了所有我想探讨的主题。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的或者想给听众留下的东西吗？

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Yeah. We've spent a lot of time talking about intensity and the grind, and the need to just always be operating at the 99th percentile. And I think if you listen to that in a vacuum, it's very easy to believe that that intensity is soul crushing, that it's a negative, that it's maybe not something that you want. And I think there's a backstop for me that I didn't talk about today that I think is important to share, which is that life is amazing. That the fact that we all exist on this blue marble drifting through space and time, that we are some weird instantiation of consciousness, each of us, and that you're here for such a short period of time whittling your stick, doing something, that if you remember how insignificant we are and all of this is, it brings this levity to what we do and to the work we put into building this. (01:27:47): Because Silicon Valley in 2025 is Florence and the Renaissance. It's crazy. The amount of creativity and insane invention and progress that's happening for our species right now in this place is absolutely unparalleled in all human history. You've got to zoom out and appreciate that magic. And so then you turn around and you're like, fuck, I've got to work on Friday night, right? I've got to go give it my all. I've got to go compete in the arena of business. (01:28:22): You have to never forget that number one, none of this matters. And number two, it is an absolutely beautiful and amazing phenomenon that we get to be alive doing this right now. So play the sport, play it with everything you've got, but never forget that it's just a sport and that none of it matters. I think it's super important as a counterpoint to the intensity that we talked about.
turns.zh:
是的。我们花了很多时间讨论专注力和奋斗精神，以及必须始终保持99%水准的需求。如果单纯从这个角度看，很容易认为这种专注力令人精疲力竭，是种负面因素，根本不是我们想要的。但今天我没提到的一点很重要，那就是生命本身就是奇妙的。我们存在于这个漂浮在时空中的蓝色星球上，每个人都是意识的奇特具象化身，生命如此短暂，我们要不断雕刻自己的木棍，努力做事。如果能意识到我们是多么渺小，所有这一切又多么微不足道，这会为我们的工作和奋斗注入轻松感。
（01:27:47）因为2025年的硅谷将是文艺复兴时期的佛罗伦萨。太不可思议了。人类历史上从未有过像现在这样在科技领域创造力爆炸、疯狂发明和进步的时刻。我们必须跳出局限，欣赏这种奇迹。然后你又会想，天哪，周五晚上还要加班，对吧？我必须全力以赴，在商业战场上竞争。
（01:28:22）永远记住，第一，这都不重要。第二，我们能活着见证这一切，实在是太美妙了。所以尽情投入比赛，但别忘了这只是场比赛，一切都不重要。我觉得这和我们谈论的专注力形成了很好的平衡。

turns.speaker: Matt MacInnis
turns.en: Okay. Two or three books. You give me a heads-up on this. So one book is Conscious Business. I don't have Conscious Business in front of me because it's actually at the office because we have Conscious Business Reading Club at Rippling. It was recommended to me by Bryan Schreier at Sequoia when he was on my board at my previous company. I took way too long to take him up on the advice, wished I had read it sooner. Highly recommend Conscious Business. Changes your life. (01:30:01): Number two, Thinking in Systems, Donna Meadows. I always mispronounce her name, Donella Meadows.
